title: Serbia's longtime strongman Vucic concedes election defeat to student-led opposition
summary: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power ​and heralds a new political era in the ​Balkan country.

image.caption: Former Serbian president Aleksandar Vucic, a candidate for prime minister, concedes defeat in the country's parliamentary election during a speech in Belgrade on Sunday. (Zorana Jevtic/Reuters)

blocks.text: Serbia's Aleksandar Vucic conceded defeat to a student-led protest movement in a historic election on Sunday that ends his long grip on power ​and heralds a new political era in the ​Balkan country.
Streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration after ex-leader's announcement
The streets of Belgrade erupted in celebration after Vucic's announcement, with cars honking and students shouting "victory" and "he's done."

The snap ​election came after almost two years of student-led demonstrations against ⁠perceived corruption and creeping ⁠authoritarianism triggered by the deaths of ‌16 people when a train station canopy collapsed in the city of Novi Sad in 2024.

"Dear Serbia, tonight the voice of the people is being heard," said Radomir Sajcic, a professor at ⁠Belgrade University, speaking on behalf of the students at their headquarters. "Tonight we celebrate victory, tomorrow we build the future."

Turnout in the election was nearly 70 per cent, ‌the highest since the break-up of Yugoslavia in 1992. Lines snaked from polling stations in cities and towns across Serbia on Sunday, in a sign of widespread desire for change.

"It is clear that ​we have lost these elections, the Student List has won, they will have between 135 and ⁠140 seats and we will have 105, no one else has entered ⁠parliament," Vucic said, basing his projection off preliminary results.

A representative sample by ⁠the ⁠CESID-IPSPS pollsters showed the students' ​candidate list will have 138 deputies, while Vucic's SNS party garnered 104 seats ​in the 250-seat parliament. Remaining ⁠seats will be shared between ethnic national minority parties.
"Unbelievable happiness and joy and we have finally got rid of this mafia. I am so happy I cannot speak," said a woman named Tanja who was celebrating on the streets ⁠of Belgrade.
